verdict.callLine: The Data Center growth is real. So is the earnout tax on every AI headline this stock trades on.

tiles.fact: Data Center revenue up 46% YoY, guided to accelerate further into Q3
Three of the last four earnings prints moved the stock more than 10% in a single session, in both directions
GAAP EPS ran 65% below non-GAAP EPS this quarter, largely stock comp and an earnout tied to Marvell's own share price
79% of revenue is now Data Center; Communications and other shrank sequentially
Net debt is a modest $1.0B against $18.5B of equity, but goodwill jumped $2.8B in one quarter on a stock-funded deal
Priced between my base and bull cases after today's drop

scored.fact: Data Center +46% YoY, guided to accelerate
GAAP EPS diluted by a self-referential earnout
One segment carries the whole story
Low net leverage, but goodwill-heavy after Celestial
Between base and bull after today's selloff

working: Data Center revenue is genuinely accelerating — 46% year-over-year, 18% sequentially, and management guided Q3 revenue to $3.15B, another double-digit sequential step up.
NVIDIA put $2.0B of real money into Marvell as a strategic investor, not just a customer, via convertible preferred stock struck well below today's price.
Net leverage is low — about $1.0B of net debt against $18.5B of stockholders' equity — and every senior note is laddered years out with no near-term maturity wall.
There is a real, dated catalyst ahead: management's own Investor Day on {wd.investorDayDate}, where it plans to lay out the long-term AI infrastructure strategy in detail.
Every quarter for at least two years has beaten its own guidance midpoint — the execution track record on the number the company controls is intact.
watch: Q3 FY27's guided non-GAAP gross margin (57.5%-58.5%) sits below Q2's actual 58.9% — margin, not revenue, is what actually moved the stock today.
The Celestial earnout is a bet on Marvell's own stock price, not on Celestial's business — 'not material' revenue so far, and a liability that grows precisely when the stock does.
Communications and other revenue fell 3% sequentially even as Data Center masked it — a second data point here and this becomes a real crack, not a rounding error.
Distributor A now accounts for 37% of net revenue, up from 24% two fiscal years ago — a concentration that keeps climbing.

Seven executives have sold $48.1M combined over 16 months and bought nothing on their own initiative — most on pre-set plans, but that is a lot of one-way conviction from the people who see the numbers first.
why: The growth is concentrated but real. Data Center is 79% of Marvell now and it is the only segment actually accelerating — that is a legitimate AI-infrastructure story, not a headline.

The earnings quality has a self-inflicted wound. A $3.5B acquisition structured with a stock-price-linked earnout has already cost $302.7M of GAAP earnings in two quarters — money spent managing an accounting exposure the company created by how it wrote the deal.
The price already needs a lot to go right. At {price|$} the stock sits between my base and bull cases — today's drop bought you a slightly better entry, not a cheap one.
A decent price for me: {fair.mid|$} or lower. That is roughly the midpoint of a model that already assumes Data Center keeps compounding — near it or below, the odds start working for you.

notes.findings: COLD OPEN, to camera before the deck: Marvell just beat every single number on its earnings report and raised its outlook again — and the stock fell double digits today anyway. That does not make sense until you read what is actually in the filings. Four things buried in the 10-Q and the fine print explain what the headline beat does not. THEN the slide: here they are. TARGET 24s.
notes.scoreboard: First, the quarter as reported yesterday after the close. Revenue two point seven three nine billion, a record, up thirty seven percent year over year. Non-GAAP earnings ninety four cents a share, comfortably ahead of estimates. But look at the GAAP number right next to it: thirty three cents. Less than half. That gap is not just stock comp — there's something else in there, and we're about to find it. TARGET 24s.
notes.reaction: Finding one. Marvell's stock does not trade on whether it beats guidance — it always beats guidance, by a little, like clockwork. Every single quarter for the last eight has landed above the midpoint the company set three months earlier. Today's beat, thirty nine million dollars, was the biggest of the last seven quarters. And the stock still fell more than ten percent. Look at the pattern across two years: reactions ranging from plus twenty three percent to minus twenty percent, with no relationship at all to how big the beat was. What actually moved it today was three lines down in the outlook: next quarter's margin guide, which came in below what the company just delivered. TARGET 30s.
notes.segments: Finding two. Marvell reports one blended growth number, thirty seven percent. That hides what's actually happening underneath. Data Center revenue: up forty six percent year over year, now seventy nine percent of the entire company. Everything else — enterprise networking, carrier infrastructure, consumer — actually shrank three percent from the quarter before. This is not a broad-based beat. It is one segment, growing very fast, carrying every other part of the business on its back. TARGET 28s.
notes.celestial: Finding three, and this is the one that explains the GAAP-to-non-GAAP gap from the scoreboard slide. In February, Marvell paid three and a half billion dollars for a company called Celestial AI — fifty five percent of it in stock, twenty four and a half million new shares. Celestial's revenue so far: the filing's own words, 'not material.' But here's the part nobody flagged: part of that deal is an earnout, and its accounting value is modeled off Marvell's OWN stock price. As the stock ran up on AI headlines this year, that liability swelled — three hundred two million dollars of GAAP earnings drag in just two quarters, net of a hedge Marvell had to go buy specifically to manage the exposure it created. That's real money spent managing an accounting mechanism, not the business. TARGET 32s.
notes.nvidia: Finding four. Buried in the same note as the Celestial earnout: on March thirty first, NVIDIA bought two billion dollars of Marvell preferred stock. Convertible into common shares at ninety one dollars and eighty four cents each. Marvell trades today well over double that. NVIDIA is not just designing chips with Marvell — it is sitting on a stake that is already deeply in the money, and almost nobody covering this earnings report mentioned it. TARGET 26s.
notes.insider: One more thing, and it took the most digging of anything in this episode: every Form 4 Marvell's executives and directors have filed in the last sixteen months, re-parsed by hand because no single filing adds this up. Seven people sold stock — the CEO, the COO, the Data Center president, the general counsel, and both the outgoing and incoming CFO — forty eight million dollars combined. Most of it, about eighty percent, was on a pre-set trading plan scheduled months ahead, which is the fair, boring explanation for most insider selling. But one sale wasn't on any plan: the brand new CFO, eight days into the job, sold shares with no 10b5-1 plan cited anywhere in the filing. And here's the part that actually surprised me: in sixteen months, the only shares anyone bought were twenty seven thousand two hundred shares, picked up by four executives on the exact same day, at the exact same price — a routine paycheck stock-purchase plan, not a single person deciding this was a good time to buy. Seven sellers. Zero real buyers. TARGET 32s.
notes.peers: So what are you paying for this? Same yardstick for everyone: market value against the latest reported quarter, annualized, growth right beside it. Against Broadcom — the closest direct comparison in custom AI silicon — Marvell trades at a real discount per dollar of sales. But check growth before you call that cheap: Marvell is growing meaningfully slower than Broadcom right now. A real discount, against a real growth gap — on a growth-adjusted basis the two are closer than the sticker price alone suggests. TARGET 24s.
notes.call: So here's the whole story on one ruler. My model: a rough case if Data Center growth cools and margins keep compressing, a base case if the current trajectory holds, and a bull case that needs Marvell to keep compounding Data Center at close to today's pace with real margin expansion. Today's price sits between my base and bull cases — the ten percent drop bought you a better entry, not a cheap stock. Everything genuinely working here — the Data Center growth, NVIDIA's own money, the low leverage — is mostly already in the price. What's not fully priced: three hundred two million dollars a year of accounting noise from one earnout, and a second segment that just went negative. My call is WATCH. My line is on the ruler, halfway between base and bull. That's the fundamentals — now let's go to the chart.
